strengths: Clear motivation with effective illustrations comparing static vs. dynamic trajectory generalization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 D4RL tasks with diverse baselines and ablation studies
Thorough ablation analysis (Figure 3) and parameter sensitivity studies (Table 2) validating component contributions
Modular framework design with clear separation of concerns (retrieval, step estimation, diffusion)
Honest discussion of limitations and failure modes (e.g., poor performance on sparse HalfCheetah dataset)
Training curve analysis (Figure 4) consistently demonstrates retrieval benefits across environments
weaknesses: Marginal and inconsistent performance: RAD (81.2) underperforms ReDiffuser (82.6) and matches DD (81.8)—claimed superiority not supported by results
Critical fundamental limitation: method fails on sparse/noisy datasets (HalfCheetah) with no principled solution, only vague future work suggestions
State embedding source unspecified: unclear if pre-trained, learned, or frozen—critical for retrieval quality but not addressed
Retrieval-inference mismatch: training uses pseudo-targets from dataset trajectories, but inference retrieves arbitrary states—potential distribution shift not analyzed
Step estimation trained on ground-truth trajectory offsets but applied to arbitrary retrieved state pairs at inference; robustness unclear
Missing key technical details: return predictor Jϕ training completely unspecified, guidance scaling ρ not ablated, tolerance threshold η not studied
Limited novelty: combination of existing techniques (retrieval, diffusion conditioning, state anchoring) without strong theoretical or empirical justification
No comparison to trajectory augmentation methods (e.g., SER) despite extensive motivation criticizing augmentation approaches
High variance and small sample sizes: large error bars (e.g., ±12.7 for Hopper), only 3 random seeds, no statistical significance testing
Narrow experimental scope: only continuous control on D4RL; no discrete actions, image observations, or other benchmarks; no explicit OOD/distribution shift evaluation
Incomplete ablations: missing ablation for guidance strength ρ, filter tolerance η, return predictor quality, and embedding source
Pseudo-target training strategy lacks justification: why does seeing random offsets teach the model to reach *specific* retrieved targets?

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (locomotion, navigation, manipulation) with proper baseline selection and strong results on 16/18 D4RL datasets, particularly on navigation tasks (8.7 point improvement on AntMaze-Medium-Play)

Thorough ablation studies (Section 5.3) with clear analysis of component contributions, distribution shift experiments (Tables 2-3) demonstrating improved OOD generalization, and extensive appendices with parameter studies and sensitivity analyses

Well-motivated problem formulation with effective visualization (Figure 1) of distribution shift limitations in static augmentation approaches, and practical solution with interpretable design (retrieving states from existing trajectories)

Addresses computational overhead through periodic replanning achieving 77% wall-clock time reduction with minimal performance loss (Table 14), and provides clear algorithms and implementation details supporting reproducibility

Two variants (D-RAD, DL-RAD) compatible with different generative models, honest discussion of fundamental limitations (dataset coverage dependency), and visualization of retrieved targets providing interpretability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—combines existing techniques (diffusion models, similarity retrieval, step classification) without conceptually new insights; step estimation reformulation (Eq. 5-6) lacks theoretical justification for converting regression to classification via Sigmoid + argmax

Fundamental and inadequately analyzed dependency on high-return expert trajectories in dataset—method falls back to backbone when targets unavailable, but frequency and impact of fallback not quantified; severely limits applicability to low-quality datasets

Concept of 'reachability' neither formally defined nor guaranteed—target selection uses same-trajectory, H-1 step heuristic without ensuring agent can actually reach targets; limited visualization (Figure 4) in single environment

Hyperparameter proliferation with non-monotonic sensitivity—δ (similarity threshold), η, k (top-k), H, τ require environment-specific tuning; different settings across variants (top-6 vs. top-500) without principled guidance for new domains; Tables 9-10 show inconsistent sensitivity

Incremental and inconsistent improvements—typical gains only 5-10%, underperforms MOPO on HalfCheetah distribution shifts (62.3 vs 39.2), minimal gains on Medium-Expert datasets, and some Maze2D configurations underperform baselines; questions robustness

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive baselines, ablations, and supplementary analyses across diverse D4RL environments, demonstrating competitive performance on 16/18 datasets with substantial gains on long-horizon tasks like AntMaze.
Clear problem motivation effectively illustrated (Figure 1) for why static data augmentation fails for OOD states and why dynamic target selection could help.
Thoughtful engineering including trajectory-length-based target selection, pseudo-target randomization strategy, and two method variants (D-RAD/DL-RAD) compatible with different diffusion frameworks.

Thorough empirical analysis with ablation studies validating component contributions, OOD generalization tests showing improvements on distribution shifts, and visualization confirming target feasibility.
Strong results on navigation benchmarks (AntMaze) with 86.7 on Medium-Play vs. 78.0 for DiffuserLite baseline.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (retrieval + diffusion planning) with no fundamental algorithmic innovations. Each component (similarity search, return filtering, MLP classifier for step estimation) is standard.

Overstated OOD generalization claims contradicted by paper's own acknowledgments: 'RAD still relies on the coverage of the offline dataset. When high-return target states are absent, the planning...is ineffective' (Section 6). This fundamental limitation undermines the central motivation about handling OOD scenarios.

Insufficient theoretical justification: Appendix E entropy proof is trivial (chain rule of conditional entropy), no characterization of when RAD should work vs. fail, and missing formal analysis of why target-conditioning should improve policy generalization beyond reducing entropy.

Mixed generalization results undermine universal applicability: Table 2 shows DL-RAD substantially underperforms MOPO on HalfCheetah Medium-Replay (39.2 vs 62.3), dismissed with vague post-hoc explanations rather than systematic analysis.

Methodological concerns: (1) 'Expert trajectory' definition is vague and task-dependent (e.g., arbitrary length thresholds); (2) Inconsistent baseline configurations (SER/DiffStitch use IQL as backbone); (3) Database restricted to experts may miss useful intermediate states.

Multiple design choices lack principled justification: trajectory-length selection (Table 16 shows modest gains; why not learned scoring?), pseudo-target random offset strategy (post-hoc explanation), step estimation reformulated as classification with argmax (what about between-class cases?), and multiple hyperparameters (δ, η, k, H) with sensitivity shown but no selection procedure.

Significant practical limitations: +0.20s per-step overhead (Table 5), 1.4GB memory footprint for indices, periodic replanning workaround suggests computational concerns not fundamentally addressed, and hyperparameter tuning complexity.

Reproducibility issues: code link incomplete, different environment-specific tuning required (Table 6), hyperparameter selection procedure undescribed, and sensitivity to similarity metric choice (Section D.7) raises consistency concerns.

Weak related work engagement: missing connections to goal-conditioned RL and hindsight experience replay, limited discussion of when retrieval is theoretically beneficial in offline RL, and comparison with closest related work (DiffStitch) relegated to appendix.

Incomplete failure analysis: limited characterization of when/why method fails, Table 3 shows catastrophic failure (0.0 across baselines) in some settings without explanation, and missing ablations on retrieval database composition and inverse dynamics quality.

strengths: Clear problem motivation with effective intuition (Figure 1) for why dynamic target selection overcomes static augmentation limitations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4+ benchmark suites (D4RL, OGBench, navigation, manipulation) with best/near-best on 16/18 datasets
Particularly strong results on navigation tasks (AntMaze +8.7 over DiffuserLite) and generalization to severe OOD scenarios (Table 3: 36.7 when baselines fail)
Thorough ablation studies clearly demonstrating component contributions, including comparison with random targets and pseudo-target strategy justification
Rigorous distribution shift experiments (Tables 2-3) showing practical generalization beyond training distribution
Honest computational analysis with practical solutions (periodic planning reduces 4× overhead by 77% with minimal performance loss)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, implementation details, and promised code release
Visualization validation (Figure 4) demonstrating retrieved targets are reasonable and reachable in practice
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (standard retrieval, heuristic target selection, existing diffusion models) without significant methodological innovation
Fundamental limitation acknowledged but unsolved: method depends on high-return state coverage in dataset; becomes ineffective when such states are absent

Inconsistent improvements: marginal gains on Medium-Expert datasets (~1-3%) and performance degradation vs. MOPO on HalfCheetah under distribution shift, suggesting method doesn't universally improve generalization

Ad-hoc design choices lack principled justification: selection of longest-remaining-trajectory criterion (Eq. 4) is intuitive but arbitrary; classification vs. regression for step estimation not empirically compared
Significant computational overhead: 4× inference time increase per step (0.06s→0.26s in AntMaze); periodic replanning adds implementation complexity and is not always practical
Return value computation underspecified: unclear how discounted returns are computed in practice, especially critical for sparse-reward navigation tasks where return differentiation is unclear
Narrow experimental scope: all evaluations on D4RL/OGBench synthetic environments; no real robotic or domain-specific offline RL applications tested
Step Estimation module details sparse: inverse dynamics model training procedure not described; potential for error propagation not addressed; classification formulation not compared to alternatives
Training-testing mismatch: random offset during training (Eq. 12) vs. fixed offset during testing could impact generalization; stability of gradient term ∇J_ϕ not discussed
